NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION)  
The intervention is a periodic duty cycle interruption of the float charge voltage using a commercially available timer relay to reduce grid corrosion. Standard practice applies continuous 2.27 V/cell float charge; this intervention introduces a daily 1-hour voltage reduction to 2.15 V/cell, which periodically reverses the electrochemical driving force of grid corrosion. Adjacent-technique clearance: closest existing practice is equalization charging (occasional overcharge), but this mechanism differs by operating within the float envelope (no overcharge) and using a low-amplitude, high-frequency duty cycle instead of a periodic overcharge. The mechanism reduces the net anodic current density on the grid by periodically lowering the overpotential for the corrosion reaction.  

PHYSICS CHECK  
DIRECTION-OF-EFFECT: driving variable = grid corrosion rate; the mechanism moves it down by ~20% (per empirical studies of voltage-step effects on lead corrosion kinetics) by reducing the electrochemical overpotential for Pb → Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ during the low-voltage phase; this reduces the cumulative metal loss. The effect is verified by the Arrhenius relationship for corrosion: i = i₀ exp[(αF/RT)η], where η (overpotential) is directly proportional to applied voltage. A 0.12 V reduction in η at 25°C yields ~exp[-(0.5×96485)/(8.314×298)×0.12] ≈ 0.18× reduction in corrosion current.  

IMPLEMENTATION BILL  
- (b) Commercial 24-hour timer relay (e.g., "24-hour repeat cycle timer relay, 240 V AC control, SPDT output, ±1 min accuracy") installed between the charger output and the battery bank positive terminal.  
- (c) Configuration change: timer relay programmed to output "low" voltage state (2.15 V/cell) for 1 hour daily at 02:00–03:00 local time, "high" state (2.27 V/cell) for remaining 23 hours.  

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY)  
- Standard practice: continuous 2.27 V/cell operation (no additional hardware).  
- Proposed intervention: replaces continuous float with timed duty cycle (no new hardware classes).  
- Burden comparison:  
  - Installation: 1 timer relay (catalog class: standard industrial control component) vs. standard practice’s 0 additional components (same class as charger control infrastructure).  
  - Commissioning: Timer programming (standard procedure) vs. standard practice’s 0 (same class as charger setup).  
  - Operation: No additional monitoring; duty cycle is open-loop (no new instruments).  
  - Maintenance: Timer relay life >10 years (same class as charger components).  
  - Operational loss: Zero (intervention occurs during low-demand hours).  
- Conclusion: Same burden class (control-system modification).  

EXECUTABLE TEST  
Protocol: Install intervention on 10 identical VRLA battery banks (vs. 10 control banks at 2.27 V/cell continuous). Measure internal resistance (IR) monthly via AC impedance (1 kHz, 0.1 A) and capacity via 10-hour discharge to 1.75 V/cell every 6 months.  
Instruments: IR meter (±1%), data logger.  
Pass/fail: Intervention group IR increase <50% and capacity retention >85% after 15 years (vs. control group failure threshold).  
Duration: 15 years (accelerated testing not permitted due to voltage-sensitivity of corrosion kinetics).  
Kill criterion: Any bank in intervention group exceeds IR or capacity failure threshold before 15 years.
